units.title: Aortic Valve Anatomy, Cusp Number and Function, the Surface Area and Normal Systolic Physiology
units.sec: Aortic Valve Anatomy, Cusp Number and Function, the Surface Area and Normal Systolic Physiology
units.guide:
The aortic valve has three equal cusps and three commissures around one fibrous annulus; its surface area is 3–4 cm² (p307).
Cusps are crescent shaped, open fully for unimpeded flow and close tightly against regurgitation; congenital counts are four (quadricuspid), two (BAV) or one (unicuspid), and fewer cusps favour stenosis over regurgitation, with BAV stenosis 75% against regurgitation 20–25%.
Normal systole runs IVC → aortic and pulmonary valves open → rapid then reduced ejection; LVP and aortic pressure are each 120 mmHg, so a completely opening valve produces no gradient.

units.sec: The Aortic-Sclerosis-to-Stenosis Pathogenesis Chain, Rheumatic Valve Combinations, Demographic Notes, Specimen Captions and Etiology
units.guide:
A bicuspid or tricuspid valve plus a pathological process gives aortic sclerosis; inflammation and lipoprotein deposition lead into the atherosclerotic process of RAAS activation, myofibroblast-to-osteoblast change and calcium hydroxyapatite deposition (p308).
Adding a transvalvular gradient turns sclerosis into aortic stenosis and symptoms; rheumatic combinations are MS + MR (m/c), MS + AR (2nd m/c) and AR + AS, while 30% of elderly have non-severe sclerosis, 80% of patients are male and valve replacement requires coronary angiography.
The four captions cover BAV calcific stenosis, L/R cusp fusion with a calcified noncoronary cusp, TAV stenosis with fused commissures and the 1 cm scale; degenerative calcification is the worldwide AS cause, BAV in the young, aortic sclerosis the commonest valvular pathology and MR the commonest valvular heart disease, with rheumatic AS less common.

units.title: Bicuspid Aortic Valve Genetics and Aortopathy, Location-Based Types, Severity-Based Types and the 40/4/1 Rule
units.sec: Bicuspid Aortic Valve Genetics and Aortopathy, Location-Based Types, Severity-Based Types and the 40/4/1 Rule
units.guide:
BAV is the commonest congenital valve defect, linked to NOTCH-1 and eNOS defects, M > F, autosomal dominant inheritance and aortopathies (aneurysm and dissection) requiring CT aortogram before valve replacement (p309).
Location types are valvular AS, subvalvular AS with HCM and supravalvular AS with Williams syndrome (increased calcium, growth failure and mental retardation); mild/moderate disease stays asymptomatic through concentric LVH that preserves cardiac output at the expense of cavity size.
Severe AS has symptoms, a 1% sudden-death risk and needs valve replacement, with the 40/4/1 rule of mean gradient >40 mmHg, peak velocity >4 m/s and area <1 cm²; very severe AS gives LV failure and a bad prognosis, and the gradient exists because the stenotic valve does not open completely.

units.title: The ASD 5/3/1 Symptom Clock, Angina, Syncope and Dyspnea Mechanisms, Association Notes, Pulse, Blood Pressure, JVP and Apex
units.sec: The ASD 5/3/1 Symptom Clock, Angina, Syncope and Dyspnea Mechanisms, Association Notes, Pulse, Blood Pressure, JVP and Apex
units.guide:
The ASD symptom clock prints angina 5 years, syncope 3 years and dyspnea 1 year for valve replacement (p310). Angina comes from increased LV mass/oxygen demand, reduced coronary flow with atherosclerosis and reduced capillary density relative to wall thickness; syncope is a fixed cardiac output that fails to rise with activity.
Dyspnea follows concentric LVH → smaller cavity → raised LVEDP/LAP/PCWP → pulmonary exudation. AF is called fatal because the atria contribute 40% of CO when LVEDP is high; systemic HTN masks severity and needs tight control; LV failure marks very severe AS and complete gradient loss is low-flow low-gradient AS; Heyde syndrome and acquired von Willebrand disease are added.
Severe AS has pulsus tardus (slow rise but reaches amplitude) and very severe AS pulsus parvus et tardus (does not reach amplitude); LVF narrows pulse pressure, JVP remains normal and the LVH apex is displaced outward and heaving.

units.title: Heart Sounds and the Mixed-Frequency Murmur with Its Carotid and Apical Components, ECG, X-Ray and ECHO
units.sec: Heart Sounds and the Mixed-Frequency Murmur with Its Carotid and Apical Components, ECG, X-Ray and ECHO
units.guide:
Heart sounds on p311 include an ejection click in BAV, soft S2 in degenerative disease, loud S2 in BAV and reverse-split S2 (late A2) in severe AS, with S3 from LVH/LVF and S4 present.
The murmur is a harsh mixed-frequency ejection systolic murmur with late systolic accentuation that separates it from an innocent ESM; its low-pitch component radiates to the carotid and its high-pitch component to the apex (Gallavardin phenomenon), and it is best heard in the aortic area.
Investigations show an LV strain pattern with Sokolov–Lyon >35 mm, not much ST depression and asymmetric T inversion on ECG, a dilated aortic arch on X-ray, and ECHO as the definitive test that also grades severity.

units.title: Aortic Valve Replacement and Its Indications, Dobutamine Stress Testing, Disadvantages, TAVR and the Two Transcatheter Valves
units.sec: Aortic Valve Replacement and Its Indications, Dobutamine Stress Testing, Disadvantages, TAVR and the Two Transcatheter Valves
units.guide:
AVR commonly uses a bioprosthetic valve because it causes fewer complications and avoids continued anticoagulation (p312). Indications are severe symptomatic AS; severe asymptomatic AS with EF <50%, gradient >60 mmHg or peak flow ≥5 m/s; rapid progression on yearly echo; another planned procedure; or symptoms on a dobutamine stress test that separates very severe AS from LVF with incidental AS.
AVR disadvantages are more complications and difficulty obtaining fitness in elderly patients. TAVR is performed by a trained cardiologist, is costly and can be considered when AVR is contraindicated; the illustrated valve types are balloon-expandable and self-expanding.
